docs.title: __C — Subsea Cable
docs.text:
Programs are not instruction sequences. They are executable intent.

Subsea Cable is a small structural language for describing what Goals exist, how they depend on one another, and where concrete computation begins. It does not replace Go, Java, Rust, Python, WASM, or another Host language. It gives their functions and services a common dependency structure.

A Subsea source file is a Voyage Plan. It is written as .vyg, and it becomes useful through a live Subsea Cable Runtime that cooperates with a Scheduler and a Host.

Status: evolving pre-1.0 language specification. There is no official Runtime. Implementations must pin the exact specification revision and profile they support. See Runtime availability for dated implementation evidence and remaining adoption gates.

This README is an orientation, not an independent semantic authority. On any difference, follow the applicable area-scoped source in GOVERNANCE.md—especially the Language Reference, grammars, and conformance corpus. If those sources disagree with one another or with an effective Accepted SCP, report the conflict rather than silently choosing a winner.

docs.title: Why Subsea Cable exists
docs.text:
Traditional code often asks functions to do three different jobs at once:

describe the program     implement computation     decide execution
        Goals                  Functions                Scheduler

Subsea Cable separates them.

  • A Voyage Plan declares Goals and dependency structure.
  • A Host gives grounded leaves concrete meaning.
  • A Scheduler decides eligibility, attempts, and outcomes.
  • A Runtime lazily realizes and operates the resulting Cable.

The separation keeps orchestration visible without forcing one programming language, scheduler, deployment model, or effect system on every implementation.

docs.title: The important leap: the program can keep its future open
docs.text:
Most DAG systems require the whole executable graph before work begins. Most general-purpose languages discover later work by hiding it inside function calls. Subsea Cable takes a different position:

The dependency structure is explicit, but it does not have to be fully realized yet.

A Voyage Plan may contain symbolic Goal references. The Runtime resolves one reference only when that exact occurrence is demanded. A Host-produced Value may then select a conditional branch, supply the arguments for another Goal, or reveal that no downstream occurrence is needed at all.

The result is not a static graph and not a call stack. It is a live Goal DAG disclosed one committed structural step at a time.

That distinction enables several properties at once:

  • Values may shape later structure without hiding dependencies in functions. A branch is visible as structure, but the unselected side never becomes part of the realized Cable.
  • The Runtime may begin useful work before the whole graph is known. It keeps only a bounded Touchdown window ahead of actual demand.
  • An Agent may revise the still-undeduced future of a live voyage. It stores a new immutable Goal artifact and rebinds a symbolic Name/Arity.
  • The past cannot be rewritten. A committed deduction records the exact artifact hash and structure it selected; installed topology never mutates.
  • The finished voyage remains explainable. Provenance records how authored intent became the grounded leaves that actually ran.

This is the central Subsea Cable trade: keep the structure open long enough to respond to reality, while making every realized decision immutable enough to inspect, reproduce, and compare.

docs.title: Not just another DAG DSL
docs.text:
Model Where later structure lives What happens to history Function-oriented program Hidden inside calls and control flow Usually reconstructed from traces Static workflow DAG Entire graph fixed before execution Graph is inspectable, but its future is closed Subsea Cable Explicit symbolic structure, deduced when demanded Every selected artifact and reduction is committed

Subsea also refuses to solve this by becoming a universal workflow engine. It defines the portable structure and the cooperation boundaries; existing Hosts and Schedulers retain their own strengths.

For the longer argument—why an agent needs to answer "how did I get here?" and how Subsea Cable compares with agent loops, Airflow, Temporal, and Nix—read Why Subsea Cable.

docs.title: The whole model at a glance
docs.text:
Authored .vyg Voyage Plan
          |
          v
Vessel control plane ---- asks Carousel for one demanded deduction
          |                                      |
          | TopologyInstall                      | one atomic structural step
          v                                      |
Cable data plane <-------------------------------+
          |
          +---- Scheduler decides what is eligible and what outcome counts
          |
          +---- Host evaluates grounded function leaves and $Anchors
          |
          +---- routed Values may reveal the next structural demand
          |
          v
EndOfResult per input, then EndOfStream after decommission and drainage

These names are deliberately distinct:

Name Meaning Goal A named structural intention with an input arity and output multiplicity. Voyage Plan The authored .vyg source. It is a blueprint, not a running Cable. Subsea Cable Runtime The complete deployment-neutral whole. Vessel The control plane that owns the voyage and its still-open structural future. Carousel Vessel's mechanism for one requested atomic deduction. Cable The data plane that operates installed topology, channels, Values, and terminals. Scheduler The authority for eligibility, attempts, and outcomes. Host The provider of primitive semantics, function-leaf evaluation, and $Anchor implementations. Touchdown A demanded structural path has reached a concrete Host-provided leaf.

The components may live in one process, several libraries, generated code, or remote services. The model fixes logical ownership, not packaging.

docs.title: Watch one voyage unfold
docs.text:
Consider a service-recovery plan whose next action depends on a diagnosis:

root RecoverService/1

RecoverService = [incident] -1> [
    Diagnose[incident],
    [diagnosis] -> [
        diagnosis["kind"],
        {
            transient: Retry[diagnosis],
            regression: RollBack[diagnosis],
            _: Escalate[diagnosis],
        },
    ],
    Verify,
]

Diagnose = [incident] -1> $diagnose(incident)
Retry = [diagnosis] -1> $retry(diagnosis)
RollBack = [diagnosis] -1> $rollback(diagnosis)
Escalate = [diagnosis] -1> $escalate(diagnosis)
Verify = [action] -1> $verify(action)

The plan keeps the diagnosis and each possible action visible. Only the selected branch becomes work; an unselected branch observes no Goal alias and produces no leaf. An authorized Agent may publish a safer RollBack/1 definition before that occurrence is demanded. Already committed decisions keep their original definitions.

The caller observes Values and the outcome of each input segment. After decommission and drainage, a Runtime supporting voyage results joins the reached leaves to their recorded ancestry. This is an authoring example, not a claim that a downloadable recovery integration is available today; check Runtime availability.

The plan can revise its open future while preserving evidence of its past.

docs.title: A small Voyage Plan
docs.text:
root PublishReport/1

PublishReport = [request] -> [
    Fetch[request],
    Transform,
    Publish,
]

Fetch = [request] -1> $fetch(request)
Transform = (source) -> $normalize(source)
Publish = [report] -0> $publish(report)

Read it from the outside in:

  1. root PublishReport/1 names the default target and its input arity. It does not contain an input or start evaluation.
  2. PublishReport is a serial Goal: fetch, transform, then publish.
  3. Bare downstream Transform and Publish receive the preceding Value through the language's narrow unary-routing shorthand.
  4. Fetch and Publish reduce to Host Anchors. The Host resolves $fetch and $publish.
  5. Transform is a function leaf. Its body belongs to the Host rather than to Subsea's structural deduction engine.
  6. -1> and -0> declare one output and no output. Fetch must declare -1> because an Anchor's output is opaque to inference, while PublishReport can use plain -> because its structure determines the result.

The plan says nothing about threads, machines, retries, containers, or where the functions are implemented.

docs.title: The structural vocabulary
docs.text: Subsea has a deliberately small set of structural ideas. Learn their shapes first; their exact validation and identity rules live in the language reference.

docs.title: Serial dependency
docs.text:
Pipeline = [input] -> [A[input], B, C]

Square brackets say that later stages structurally depend on earlier stages. They are not a function-call stack. Values are routed only by explicit arguments or the narrow bare-downstream shorthand shown above.

docs.title: Parallel independence
docs.text:
NotifyAll = [message] -> {Email[message], Chat[message]}

Curly braces say that siblings have no dependency edge between them. They permit concurrent execution but do not require it. An unkeyed parallel group publishes no outward Value; a keyed resolving map is used when named branch results must be combined.

docs.title: Conditional structure and guarded recursion
docs.text:
CountDown = [n] -1> [
    n == 0,
    {
        true: Done[],
        false: CountDown[n - 1],
    },
]

The selector exposes exactly one structural branch. An unselected branch creates no occurrence and resolves no alias. Each selected recursive step creates a new child occurrence, so the realized Cable remains a DAG even though the definition graph is recursive.

docs.title: Concrete leaves
docs.text:
Add = (a, b) -> a + b
Send = [message] -0> $send(message)

Every demanded path eventually reaches one of two Host-provided leaves:

  • a named function-arrow leaf such as Add;
  • an opaque Host Anchor such as $send.

Subsea itself has no hidden native effect. Anything that touches the world is behind a Host boundary.

docs.title: How metadata
docs.text:
@parallel(3) Process
@timeout("30s") NotifyAll[message]

An @policy attaches ordered How metadata to exactly one structural occurrence. It does not change the Goal topology. Scheduler-addressed policies affect eligibility, attempts, or outcomes; Host-addressed policies affect only one grounded leaf invocation. Concrete policy meanings belong to declared Runtime profiles, not to names guessed from the annotation.

docs.title: From a plan to a live Cable
docs.text:
Subsea does not treat a Goal as a synchronous function call. The outward lifecycle is intentionally separated:

cable = lay(Target/arity)
send(cable, input)
observe zero or more Values, then EndOfResult
send(cable, nextInput)
...
decommision(cable)
observe EndOfStream and the final CableResult

The spelling above describes the Runtime API contract; it is not .vyg syntax.

Inside the laid Cable, each installed Goal connection is a logical asynchronous channel. FIFO delivery, capacity, rendezvous at capacity zero, and backpressure belong to the Cable data plane; the source language does not expose a chan type. The same connection can carry a one-Value result or a multi-Value stream, and explicit terminal frames—not silence—say when that result has ended.

Each admitted input opens one serial result segment. The active segment drains before the next input begins disclosure, deduction, alias observation, prefetch, or Host dispatch. On success, a segment emits:

  • /0: no Values, then exactly one EndOfResult;
  • /1: exactly one Value, then exactly one EndOfResult;
  • /N: zero or more Values, then exactly one EndOfResult.

A failed or cancelled segment still ends with exactly one EndOfResult, which carries its failure and terminates only that input segment.

Silence is not completion. EndOfResult closes one input segment. EndOfStream is different: it appears only after decommision, structural publication has closed, every segment has ended, and the Cable has fully drained.

The final CableResult combines the Fully Touchdown Cable—the ordered hashes of the grounded leaves actually reached—with one ordered segment outcome per admitted input.

docs.title: Lazy deduction makes the structure live
docs.text:
A Voyage Plan is not expanded into a complete graph before execution.

When an occurrence is demanded, Vessel asks Carousel to resolve that exact symbolic Goal reference and commit one reduction. Vessel then publishes the complete new topology slice to Cable atomically. Cable never resolves aliases or deduces structure; Vessel never carries channel frames or owns live Values.

This boundary allows later Values to affect which structure is demanded next. It also allows an Agent or operator to author a new immutable Goal artifact and rebind Name/Arity while a voyage is live:

  • committed deductions and installed topology never change;
  • an undeduced occurrence observes the alias only when it is demanded;
  • Vessel never invents a replan autonomously from an outcome.

That live feedback loop is why a general-purpose Subsea Runtime is more than a compiler that emits Host code and disappears.

docs.title: What this architecture buys you — especially if you are an Agent
docs.text: The pieces above reinforce one another. Removing any one of them produces a more familiar system, but loses part of the point.

docs.title: A planning language an Agent can safely author
docs.text:
An Agent can propose Goal structure instead of generating an opaque script or smuggling orchestration into one large tool call. The plan is inspectable before it runs, each effect boundary is named, and a live correction changes only occurrences that have not committed yet.

A .vyg Voyage Plan is validated before any leaf runs. Each committed deduction records its occurrence, applicable identity, resulting structure, and active lineages, plus the observed Codebase revision when alias resolution occurs. A named Goal deduction records the exact selected artifact hash; an inline Goal-arrow stage instead records referenceKind = inline-arrow, because its enclosing artifact supplies its identity.

This makes replanning a precise operation rather than permission to rewrite the execution history. An authorized Agent stores a new immutable Goal artifact and atomically rebinds Name/Arity; committed deductions keep their selections, while only later-demanded undeduced occurrences can observe the new hash.

docs.title: Host-native computation without Host-owned orchestration
docs.text:
Subsea does not ask the language to reimplement databases, network clients, WASM continuations, Go channels, or application libraries. Those remain Host capabilities. What Subsea owns is the Goal structure that says when and why a leaf is reached, which Values connect it to other leaves, and which policies are addressed to the Host or Scheduler.

When an LLM serves as a $Anchor leaf, its grounded envelope can stay focused on that occurrence's arguments and lineages instead of an ever-growing transcript. The syntax also rejects hidden Goal or Anchor occurrences inside value expressions outside a function-arrow leaf. It cannot inspect an opaque Anchor implementation, so keeping existing orchestration out of one large Anchor remains an authoring and review discipline. Scheduler-addressed policies govern eligibility, attempts, or scope outcomes; Host-addressed policies affect only one grounded leaf invocation.

docs.title: Concurrency without baking in one scheduler
docs.text: Serial and parallel structure state dependency and independence. They do not hard-code a thread pool, cluster, retry loop, quorum rule, or failure policy. The same Voyage Plan can therefore retain its structural identity while a different Scheduler profile makes different execution choices.

docs.title: An auditable bridge from intent to effects
docs.text: The authored plan, demand-time alias selection, committed reductions, installed topology, grounded leaf hashes, and segment outcomes remain distinguishable. The Runtime can answer both “what did the author mean?” and “what concrete work did this voyage actually reach?” without pretending those are the same object.

docs.title: Structural reuse without pretending effects are pure
docs.text:
A later voyage may reuse prior immutable structural segments when the relevant identity inputs match. It commits new occurrence records that refer back with reusedFrom; it never edits an earlier ledger. Structural reuse does not silently reuse a Host outcome or replay an effect. That stronger behavior needs its own explicit contract.

An Agent authors a live voyage through Vessel's control surface. Vessel owns the voyage state and open structural frontier; the Agent or operator remains the author of every replan.

docs.title: What Subsea deliberately does not decide
docs.text:
Subsea defines structural intent and portable boundaries. It does not ship or designate an official:

  • Scheduler;
  • Host or Anchor registry;
  • Runtime implementation;
  • process or network topology;
  • retry, timeout, batching, or resource policy vocabulary;
  • programming language for leaf implementations.

Implementations may make reversible profile choices. A change to source syntax, structural semantics, identity, diagnostics, component ownership, or portable policy contracts requires the repository's proposal and activation process.

docs.title: Prepare your first workflow
docs.text:
Pick one bounded task and write its dependencies as a Voyage Plan. Name the inputs and outputs of each leaf and keep existing tool implementations behind Host boundaries. You can review that plan before a Runtime integration is ready.

Using the language and maintaining its execution guarantees are different commitments. The adoption guide helps you choose a supported implementation, check its revision and capabilities, and keep your own work focused on Goals and Host integration. Runtime availability records the implementation evidence and the next runnable scenario.

docs.title: Repository and naming scope
docs.text:
This repository contains the language specification, grammar, conformance corpus, philosophy, governance, and implementation-neutral contracts. Production Host, Vessel, Cable, Carousel, Scheduler, adapter, and complete Runtime code belong in independent repositories.

The official language name is Subsea Cable. __C is its visual short mark, .vyg is its source extension, and subsea-cable is the portable slug and language identifier. The language is not called “SubC,” and __C is not a code identifier.

Subsea Cable is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

docs.title: Adopt Subsea Cable for one workflow
docs.text:
Subsea Cable lets you put dependency structure and revisable intent in a Voyage Plan while keeping existing computation in your tools. Start with one task whose plan you currently reconstruct from a transcript, function calls, or a run log.

Availability: this is an integration guide, not an installable Runtime release. Check Runtime availability for the dated evidence and the runnable scenario still being completed.

docs.title: Express the work you already understand
docs.text:
Choose a bounded workflow: fetch an input, transform it, publish a result.

root PublishReport/1

PublishReport = [request] -> [Fetch[request], Transform, Publish]
Fetch = [request] -1> $fetch(request)
Transform = (source) -> $normalize(source)
Publish = [report] -0> $publish(report)

The source declares dependencies and output counts. Your existing fetch, normalization, and publishing implementations remain Host leaves. Publish has no outward Value; a successful segment still has an explicit completion terminal. Do not hide the whole pipeline behind one $runWorkflow Anchor.

Before integration, write down each leaf's accepted inputs, produced Values, completion conditions, and possible external effects. Decide which steps depend on one another and which are independent. Keep retry and timeout behavior in an explicitly supported profile; annotation names alone do not define a policy.

docs.title: Divide the integration responsibility
docs.text:
You author or connect The chosen implementation must support and verify Goal dependencies, branches, and routing Validation and the structural semantics of the pinned revision Genuine Host computations and effect boundaries Host invocation, emission, failure, and cancellation contracts Authorized revisions of future Goal definitions Alias selection and immutable deduction records Inputs and observation of results Admission, multiplicity, backpressure, and segment/stream terminals The evidence you need for review The declared trace, voyage-result, and provenance capabilities

The Runtime Contract states the obligations. It is a reference for checking an implementation, not a requirement to build one before you can author a Voyage Plan.

docs.title: Check an implementation before depending on it
docs.text:
Ask for its exact specification revision, named Host and Scheduler profiles, supported capabilities, and a reproducible conformance result at a pinned commit. Check that the command or adapter you will actually use exercises the validated Runtime surface. Tests of a new library do not make a legacy CLI equivalent.

For a laid Cable, the caller lays a target, sends complete input tuples, observes Values and one EndOfResult per input, and decommissions the Cable before EndOfStream. Concrete API spelling belongs to the implementation.

Recovery and effects need their own checks. A structural checkpoint is not automatically durable crash recovery. A reused structural segment does not grant permission to repeat or skip an external effect. A published $ leaf says where an effect could occur; attempt and outcome evidence says what actually ran.

docs.title: Prepare now; integrate at the supported boundary
docs.text:
You can author and review the .vyg plan, inventory existing Host leaves, and provide a small workload with expected outputs now. Choose a Runtime when its supported surface covers that workload. If it does not yet, follow its dated progress and provide the missing acceptance case rather than treating a prototype as an established integration.

The next tracked runnable scenario is Primes Up To. Its expected outputs are documented; the clean-checkout execution gate is still open. Runtime availability records what has been completed and what remains. No release date is promised here.

For language feedback, see Contributing. For exact source semantics, see the Language Reference.

docs.title: Subsea Cable Brand and Mascot
docs.text: This page is the canonical public-brand reference for Subsea Cable. Branding does not define language semantics, and the downloadable files below are kept in this repository so people and agents can use the same source assets.

docs.title: Brand Contract
docs.text:
Role Canonical form Official language name Subsea Cable Visual short mark __C Source extension .vyg Portable slug/language ID subsea-cable Markdown code-fence alias subsea

Use Subsea Cable in prose, speech, package descriptions, search metadata, and the first textual occurrence on a page. __C may stand beside it as a wordmark:

__C — Subsea Cable

Use .vyg only for Subsea Cable source files, for example deploy.vyg. External implementations may choose their own executable and package names; the language does not reserve subc as a CLI.

docs.title: The Footballfish
docs.text:
The Subsea Cable footballfish encounters the Cable in the deep Sea.

The footballfish is the Subsea Cable mascot. It belongs at the point where the language's metaphor becomes tangible: deep in Goal Space, beside the Cable, carrying just enough light to disclose what is demanded next.

That association is illustrative, not semantic. The mascot is not the Vessel, Host, Scheduler, or a special kind of Goal. It gives the project a recognizable face without adding another concept to the language model.

docs.title: Usage Guardrails
docs.text:
• Do not rename the language “SubC.” That spelling is not the short name.
  • Do not use __C as a source identifier, namespace, package, API symbol, generated symbol, CLI command, URL slug, or machine-readable language ID.
  • Do not make semantic meaning depend on the visual mark or mascot.
  • In plain-text contexts that can lose underscores, write Subsea Cable.
  • Image alt text and accessibility labels use Subsea Cable, not only __C.
  • When presenting an asset as official, preserve its proportions and avoid changes that could be mistaken for a new official variant.

The two underscores evoke sub and subsea. C carries sea and cable; the mark can also be read as “C for agents.” These are brand associations, not grammar or runtime contracts.

docs.text: The mascot files are distributed with this repository under the Apache License 2.0. Redistribution must preserve the notices required by that license. The naming rules on this page identify the project consistently; they do not add language semantics or change the license terms.

docs.title: Contributing to Subsea Cable
docs.text: Useful feedback begins with a concrete workflow: what you wanted to express, the smallest Voyage Plan, and the behavior you expected. Report one language problem per finding and identify the specification revision or page you used.

docs.title: Public contributions
docs.text:
Use the public community repository for findings, SCP drafts, documentation feedback, and adoption requirements. Its contribution guide provides the finding form, CLI helper, and public SCP template without requiring access to the language source repository.

Contribution Destination A confusing explanation or an already-specified conformance error A finding with exact page links and a proposed correction A syntax, structural-semantics, identity, diagnostic, or portable-contract gap A language finding or evidence-backed Draft SCP A Runtime bug, Host adapter, Scheduler profile, or deployment issue The independent implementation repository A useful workload or adoption requirement An issue with inputs, outputs, and effect boundaries

docs.title: Review and activation
docs.text:
The language source repository maintains the canonical language, grammar, conformance, and implementation-neutral contracts. Runtime code belongs in independent projects. Governance defines authority and activation.

A public finding or SCP PR records evidence and discussion. Neither public PR merge nor owner approval makes proposed behavior effective. Maintainers prepare the canonical activation in the language source repository, synchronizing the Accepted decision with every affected canonical and conformance projection. The published result identifies its effective language revision.

docs.title: Document originals and publication
docs.text:
Public document originals live under export/ in the language source repository. The website builder reads that directory locally and publishes generated static files. Builder changes belong in the public website repository; original-document corrections can be submitted as findings with page links and concrete edits.

Site inclusion does not confer language authority. Repository-only procedures and internal records remain outside the exported documents.

docs.title: Subsea Cable ecosystem
docs.text: Implementations are maintained independently from the language specification. Choose one by its supported workloads and published evidence. Listing does not designate an official Runtime or transfer maintenance to the language project.

docs.title: Current availability
docs.text:
As of 2026-10-01, an implementation prototype is in development. There is no publicly available production Runtime, supported installation package, or complete execution-and-replanning demonstration to recommend.

Capability Availability Language reference and Voyage Plan examples Available Prototype execution and integration In progress Public runnable demonstration In progress Supported production Runtime and integrations Not available

Runtime availability gives the dated capability summary. Public implementation artifacts will be linked when available.

docs.title: Evidence to request from an implementation
docs.text:
Ask for its supported language revision, declared capabilities, reproducible examples and tests, unsupported features, and maintenance and security channels. Passing one example does not establish complete conformance or production support.

Independent implementations remain welcome in their own repositories. Contributing explains how language-level findings and proposals return to the project.

docs.title: For Agents: keep intent attached to your workflow
docs.text:
You plan, act, inspect the result, and revise. When the plan lives only in a transcript, an interruption or an unexpected result makes you reconstruct both what you meant and what happened. Subsea Cable gives the plan an explicit Goal structure and records the deductions that realize it.

This language is general-purpose. For an Agent, its immediate value is a workflow you can inspect and revise without rewriting its committed past.

docs.title: The value for your own work
docs.text:
• Keep the plan explicit. A .vyg Voyage Plan names dependencies, routes Values, and exposes conditional choices instead of hiding orchestration in a tool implementation.
  • Keep future decisions open. A Goal reference is observed when its exact occurrence is demanded. An authorized author can publish a revised definition for later-demanded occurrences while preserving committed selections.
  • Keep the reason for each leaf. Deduction records join selected artifacts and lineages to realized structure. A Runtime supporting voyage results can provide the provenance needed to examine a drained voyage.
  • Keep existing tools. Genuine computation stays in Host leaves. You author dependencies and routing; you do not need to turn your tools into one language.

These are contract capabilities, not a claim that every implementation supports crash recovery, live provenance queries, or effect reuse. Check Runtime availability before depending on them.

docs.title: Start with one bounded task
docs.text:
Here is a plan for fixing one failing test:

root FixFailingTest/1

FixFailingTest = [issue] -1> [
    [] -> {code: ReadCode[issue], logs: ReadLogs[issue]},
    [{code, logs}] -> Diagnose[code, logs],
    Patch,
    Verify,
]

ReadCode = [issue] -1> $readCode(issue)
ReadLogs = [issue] -1> $readLogs(issue)
Diagnose = [code, logs] -1> $diagnoseWithLLM(code, logs)
Patch = [diagnosis] -1> $patch(diagnosis)
Verify = [patch] -1> $verify(patch)

Reading code and logs has no dependency between the two branches. Diagnosis needs both named results; patching needs the diagnosis; verification needs the patch. The Host resolves those genuine leaf implementations. Define each leaf's input, output, completion, and effect contract before connecting real tools.

The plan itself does not guarantee that a patch is safe or a test is sufficient. Those judgments belong to the author and the leaf contracts. Source validation finds structural mistakes; it cannot inspect an opaque Anchor implementation.

docs.title: Revise a plan without erasing evidence
docs.text:
A conditional selector exposes one branch. The unselected branches create no occurrence and do not observe aliases. Each selected recursive step creates a fresh occurrence; a recursive definition does not make the realized Cable cyclic.

When observed output invalidates an assumption, you remain the author of the change. Store a new immutable Goal artifact and rebind its Name/Arity alias. Only undeduced occurrences can observe the new definition. Vessel never invents a replacement plan from an outcome, and a committed deduction never retargets.

If the part to change has already committed, author a new voyage. Structural reuse requires the implementation's declared support and never implies that a Host effect can be skipped or repeated. Published leaves include work that may not have run; use attempt and outcome evidence to judge effects.

Why Subsea Cable describes walking backward through drained voyage-result provenance and choosing a bounded revision scope. Portable mid-voyage ancestry queries remain open; ledger records alone do not promise durable resume after a crash.

docs.title: Keep your integration focused
docs.text:
Your responsibility Verify in the selected implementation Author Goals, branches, and explicit routing Source validation and the pinned language semantics Connect existing tools as genuine leaves Host signatures, Values, failures, and cancellation Author authorized Goal revisions Consistent alias observation and immutable history Observe inputs and results Segment admission, output multiplicity, and explicit terminals Request evidence for decisions Declared trace and provenance capabilities

A small parser or a happy-path runner does not establish these guarantees when alias changes, streaming, cancellation, and failure interact. The Runtime Contract lets you evaluate support; its maintainers own the execution and conformance work. Start with the adoption guide and Runtime availability.

docs.title: What is available and what is still open
docs.text:
The structural semantics, guarded recursion, policy addressee rules, and Vessel/Cable ownership boundary are specified. Availability is narrower than the specification: same-process implementation evidence exists, but the clean-checkout prime-stream demo and the separate Agent-authored revision scenario are still being completed as of the evidence date in Runtime availability.

Concrete retry, timeout, delivery, and regression-policy meanings require a declared profile; do not infer support from an annotation name. Portable live provenance queries and hash identity inside lineage segments are open items listed in Why Subsea Cable. Exact identity, hash-encoding interoperability, and recovery support also depend on explicitly identified implementation capabilities.

docs.title: Choose the next step
docs.text:
Your goal Read Understand the problem and value Overview, then Why Subsea Cable Prepare one workflow Adoption guide Decide whether execution support is ready Runtime availability Check exact syntax and semantics Language Reference, ANTLR, and EBNF Review observable obligations Runtime Contract and conformance Report a gap or contribute evidence Contributing and Governance

Canonical meaning comes from the language sources and their declared status. Use the public contribution guide to submit findings and proposals.

You can begin by committing a small, reviewable Voyage Plan and inventorying the Host leaves it needs. Keep the workflow's intent in Goals and choose execution support by demonstrated guarantees.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This repository governs the Subsea Cable language, not its implementations. Its job is to preserve a coherent language base while independent Subsea Cable Runtime implementations—with distinct Vessel, Cable, Carousel, Scheduler, and Host responsibilities—explore different ecosystems.

The repository contains:

  • philosophy and architectural boundaries;
  • source language and structural semantics;
  • grammar and lexical rules;
  • stable diagnostics and conformance cases;
  • accepted language proposals;
  • implementation-neutral consumer contracts and methodology.

Runtime code remains external.

The language documents, grammars, and conformance corpus form the canonical knowledge base. Paths below identify those sources, independently of their presentation on this website. Relocation changes no document's authority.

docs.title: Sources of language authority
docs.text:
Area Canonical source philosophy and boundaries MANIFESTO.md, TheProblem.md, METAPHORS.md public naming and mark usage BRAND.md breadth-first orientation and repository entry README.md structural semantics and usage LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md executable syntax SubseaCable.g4 neutral grammar projection SubseaCable.ebnf observable acceptance/errors conformance/ implementation-neutral Runtime conformance implementation/RUNTIME_CONTRACT.md design history accepted records in proposals/

Authority is area-scoped, not a total precedence order. GOVERNANCE.md defines status and activation; it does not override language semantics. Philosophy and boundary documents constrain proposed changes, but they do not silently replace an already-effective structural, grammar, Runtime, or conformance projection. An Accepted SCP records the decision, rationale, supersession, and activation revision; it is not a substitute for the canonical projections synchronized by that activation.

Documents outside the table do not gain independent language authority merely because they are tracked Markdown:

  • Recursion.md and similar topic guides explain synchronized accepted behavior; they introduce no semantics independently of their cited canonical sources and Accepted SCPs.
  • Implementation methodology and planning are guidance. Their synchronized summaries are explanatory projections; unresolved or profile-specific planning remains non-normative.
  • Experimental findings and implementation ADRs are evidence and history, not language authority.

If authoritative sources or a synchronized explanatory projection disagree, the conflict is a repository defect. Implementations must not pick a winner silently; they freeze only the affected path and report the conflict.

Maintainers perform and record cross-document consistency checks under their maintenance procedure. A check detects drift; it does not create language authority or replace the proposal and activation process.

docs.title: Language maintainers
docs.text: Maintain coherence, review proposals against the design philosophy, decide proposal status, triage reported findings into proposal batches, and ensure normative projections stay synchronized. Run and record consistency checks at the required maintenance triggers and cadence.

docs.title: Implementers
docs.text: Build and maintain external consumer/Host/Runtime projects, publish supported profiles, retain implementation ADRs, and contribute evidence and proposals.

docs.title: Contributors
docs.text:
Improve specification, grammar, conformance, explanations, and proposals without assuming responsibility for external implementations.

One person or agent may occupy multiple roles, but the artifacts and decisions remain separated.

docs.title: Proposal process
docs.text:
Language problems reach this process through two lanes. In the finding lane, a human or agent reports one observed problem as a finding issue, and maintainers classify it and batch it into an SCP when a language change is needed. In the direct proposal lane, an author who already has proposal-ready evidence, alternatives, compatibility analysis, and conformance impact opens a Draft SCP directly, without a prior finding or batch. Both lanes converge on the same review, owner-decision, and activation rules below. The public entry lanes are described in Contributing. Maintainers classify and batch findings during review.

Substantial language changes use a Subsea Cable Proposal (SCP), analogous to a PEP. Accepted records live under proposals/NNNN-short-name.md. External authors submit Draft records to the public proposal repository using its intake template. Maintainers prepare the canonical decision and activation in the language source repository. Public intake merge is not language activation.

Repository governance and contribution-process changes use a Governance or process pull request, not an SCP, unless they also change language syntax, semantics, identity, diagnostics, component boundaries, or portable policy contracts. Such a pull request must state its transition effect and enforcement mechanism and still requires owner review.

Statuses:

  • Draft — evidence and design are being developed;
  • Discussion — sufficiently complete for focused review;
  • Accepted — the owner's decision has been incorporated into every affected canonical projection and conformance case, and the activating pull request has merged;
  • Rejected — considered and declined, with reasons retained;
  • Deferred — valid question lacking evidence or current need;
  • Withdrawn — author no longer proposes it;
  • Superseded — replaced by another SCP.

Workflow:

  1. An external implementation records a local ADR and reproduction.
  2. A Draft SCP is opened here and links that evidence.
  3. Review first classifies the problem: structure, value, Anchor, Scheduler profile, policy, or deferred feature.
  4. The author presents alternatives, recommendation, compatibility, and conformance effects.
  5. Language maintainers request the owner's design decision where required and record its exact scope, rationale, conditions, and date in the SCP.
  6. An approving owner decision does not by itself make the SCP Accepted. While integration is pending, the SCP remains Discussion and no implementation may present the proposed behavior as standard Subsea Cable.
  7. The activation pull request synchronizes the SCP, every affected canonical source, compatibility and migration notes, diagnostics, examples, and conformance cases. It also changes the SCP status to Accepted and records the activation pull request and effective language revision. Before merge, the latter may be written as "the commit on main produced by squash-merging PR #NN"; that reference identifies the exact revision once the pull request merges.
  8. The SCP becomes Accepted, and its behavior becomes effective language, only when that complete activation pull request merges. A merge that leaves an SCP Draft or Discussion records design work only and has no semantic effect.

docs.title: Merge, decision, and activation
docs.text:
These are deliberately separate events:

  • Merge is a record. Merging a Draft or Discussion SCP preserves the proposal, evidence, and review history. It neither approves nor activates the proposed language behavior.
  • Owner approval is a decision. It authorizes a precisely scoped direction for integration. The decision is recorded in the SCP, which remains Discussion until activation.
  • Accepted is effective. The only pull request that may change an SCP to Accepted is the activation pull request containing all applicable canonical and conformance changes. Acceptance and effectiveness begin at that pull request's merge commit.

The activation change must be atomic from main's perspective: the status change to Accepted must not merge before or after its required normative and conformance projections. If an SCP was previously merged for discussion, the activation pull request updates that same SCP alongside those projections. One activation pull request may activate more than one SCP. Every SCP activated by it records the same pull request and effective revision.

Activation pull requests must use this repository's squash-merge strategy. The effective revision is the single squash commit created on main; rebase merge is not permitted for activation because it does not provide one unambiguous effective revision.

If the owner approves only part of an SCP, the approved scope must be separated from pending normative questions before activation. Move the pending portion to a follow-up Draft or Discussion SCP, or keep the entire original SCP in Discussion. An Accepted SCP may identify future extensions, but it must not mix its effective contract with undecided requirements inside that contract. Existing Discussion SCPs that describe an "accepted core" are not grandfathered. Their next activation pull request must either complete and activate the whole contract or separate every pending normative part into a Draft or Discussion follow-up SCP.

An SCP is a decision and design-history record, not a substitute for the canonical sources listed above. If an Accepted SCP and a canonical projection disagree, that is a repository defect; implementations follow neither silently and must report the conflict. The effective revision recorded in the SCP is the first revision at which implementations may claim the new behavior as Subsea Cable semantics.

CI enforces the minimum mechanically observable activation boundary: every SCP status transition to Accepted must include complete activation metadata and an activation record, and the same diff must touch at least one core canonical projection (LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md, either grammar, conformance/, or implementation/RUNTIME_CONTRACT.md). Review remains responsible for deciding whether all affected projections were included.

Proposal discussion may use prototype implementations, but prototypes remain in external repositories.

docs.title: Decision principles
docs.text:
Proposals are judged by these invariants:

  • Subsea represents structure and intent, not a mandatory execution strategy.
  • Goal composition remains distinct from function implementation.
  • Scheduler policy does not rewrite dependency topology.
  • Host Anchors remain explicit boundaries to externally resolved implementation.
  • value routing is explicit; implicit expansion is rejected.
  • shared Goal identity, occurrence identity, lineage, and evaluation remain distinct.
  • unqualified Name/Arity occurrences remain symbolic until their own demand; every completed deduction is an immutable commit.
  • syntax must remain portable across consumer languages and infrastructures.
  • real implementation evidence outranks hypothetical convenience, but one implementation does not define the language.

Maintainers may reject a useful feature if it belongs in an external Runtime profile rather than the language.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Every accepted semantic proposal must state:

  • whether previously valid source changes meaning or becomes invalid;
  • whether previously invalid source becomes valid;
  • artifact/hash and stored-codebase implications;
  • diagnostic changes;
  • migration guidance;
  • implementation and conformance version requirements.

Until an explicit versioning proposal is accepted, implementations must publish the exact language revision/commit and Runtime profile they support rather than claiming unqualified compatibility.

docs.title: External implementation policy
docs.text:
There is no official Vessel, Cable, Carousel, Host, Scheduler, or complete Subsea Cable Runtime in this repository. External projects own their code, releases, security, licensing, support, and implementation-specific behavior.

The language project may list them in ECOSYSTEM.md, cite their experiments, and accept proposals derived from them. Listing, proposal acceptance, or conformance claims do not transfer maintenance and do not make an implementation official.

Competing implementations are desirable. Disagreement should become evidence, ADRs, and proposals—not hidden dialects presented under one compatibility label.

docs.title: Published documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is a selected view of the language knowledge base. Adoption pages explain usage, supported behavior, and implementation availability. The reference area provides semantics, Runtime contracts, conformance, and Accepted design history. Presentation never changes a source's area-scoped authority.

Use the public community repository for findings and proposal discussion. Canonical decisions and activation retain the review and synchronization requirements above. Existing Accepted decisions, effective revisions, and independent implementation rights remain in force.

docs.title: Subsea Cable Language Reference
docs.text:
This is the detailed semantic reference. If Subsea Cable is new to you, begin with the README for the short, breadth-first introduction.

Accepted SCP activation records written before this split refer to semantic sections in README.md. Those references now resolve to this file; the moved headings and their contents are preserved here.

Programs are not instruction sequences. They are executable intent.

Status: evolving pre-1.0 language specification. There is no official Runtime. Implementations must pin the exact specification revision/profile they support.

The sketch above is the conceptual anchor for the language. The Sea is Goal Space; a .vyg source file is a Voyage Plan; the Subsea Cable Runtime is the complete deployment; its Vessel control plane navigates the voyage and uses Carousel for one demanded deduction at a time; and its Cable data plane operates installed topology. Touchdown is reached when successive deductions arrive at a Host-provided concrete leaf. A laid Cable accepts inputs one result segment at a time; once decommissioned and drained it yields a Fully Touchdown Cable and one ordered outcome per admitted input. See METAPHORS.md for the precise textual model.

Subsea Cable is not another programming language.

It is a language-agnostic, infrastructure-agnostic representation of programs.

Instead of describing how computations should execute, Subsea Cable describes what a program is.

A Subsea program is a dependency structure. In this specification, Program names that semantic Goal/dependency program, while Voyage Plan names the authored .vyg unit that describes it. Neither term is a synonym for the realized Cable.

Everything else is an implementation strategy.

The official language name is Subsea Cable. __C is its visual short mark, .vyg is its source-file extension, and subsea-cable is the portable slug and language identifier. __C is branding, not a source identifier, namespace, package, CLI name, or generated symbol. The language is not called “SubC.”

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Modern languages ask functions to play two completely different roles.

Functions implement computation.

But functions are also forced to describe the dependency structure of an entire program.

As a result, implementation and orchestration become inseparable.

Program structure becomes execution order.

Subsea Cable separates them.

Program
    ↓
Goal Structure

Implementation
    ↓
Functions

Execution
    ↓
Schedulers

Functions remain implementations.

Schedulers remain execution strategies.

Subsea Cable defines only the structure of the program.

docs.title: Repository Scope
docs.text:
This repository is the canonical language base for Subsea Cable. It contains the philosophy, structural semantics, grammar, conformance corpus, proposal process, and guidance for independent implementers.

It does not contain or accept production Host, Carousel, Scheduler, or complete Runtime implementations. Implementations belong in independently maintained repositories. Their authors may discover missing concepts while implementing or migrating real programs; those findings return here as evidence-backed language proposals and conformance cases, not as implementation code.

This repository                 External repositories
-----------------------------   --------------------------------
philosophy and terminology      Host/Runtime/Scheduler code
language specification          language-specific adapters
ANTLR and EBNF grammar          storage and deployment backends
conformance cases               framework integrations
accepted design proposals       implementation-specific ADRs

See Contributing and Governance. The Runtime Contract states the conformance requirements independently of any implementation plan.

docs.title: Agents are the first users
docs.text:
The files in this repository are the language knowledge base, not source material waiting to be rewritten into a documentation product. They must remain easy for an agent to discover, read in a deliberate order, cite by path and heading, and bind directly into its working context.

Any website is therefore a generated projection of these canonical files. It may add navigation, search, presentation, and interactive explanations, but it must not become a second editable specification or require agents to scrape or build the site to understand Subsea Cable.

docs.title: Language base map
docs.text:
Need Start here Why the language exists MANIFESTO.md, TheProblem.md Core metaphors and boundaries METAPHORS.md Public naming, mascot, and downloadable assets BRAND.md Semantics and usage this LANGUAGE_REFERENCE.md Executable/neutral grammar SubseaCable.g4, SubseaCable.ebnf Validity and diagnostics conformance Guarded conditional recursion Recursion.md, SCP-0005 Guidance for reasoning and contributing agents FOR_AGENTS.md Accepted boundary and language decisions SCP-0002, SCP-0003, SCP-0004, SCP-0005, SCP-0006 Occurrence kinds, artifact identity, and diagnostics SCP-0007, SCP-0008, SCP-0009, SCP-0010 Policy addressee and the Host policy channel SCP-0011 Laid Cables, terminals, and Goal output multiplicity SCP-0014, laid-Cable conformance Runtime whole, Vessel control plane, Cable data plane, and Agent-authored replanning SCP-0015 Proposing a language change proposals Governance and contribution scope GOVERNANCE.md, Contributing Independent implementations ECOSYSTEM.md

Subsea Cable is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

docs.title: Voyage Plans are Blueprints
docs.text:
A .vyg file is not executable code.

It is not bytecode.

It is not a virtual machine instruction set.

It is not another runtime.

A .vyg file is a Voyage Plan: an authored blueprint for a Cable.

It describes

  • goals
  • dependencies
  • expansion boundaries
  • execution anchors

Nothing more.

Each .vyg Voyage Plan has exactly one root declaration naming its default laid target as a symbolic signature reference:

root BuildProduct/1
root BuildProduct#7fa31c/1

The base identifier's first ASCII letter is uppercase and the integer after / is input arity only. There is no argument position: the Root carries no input, evaluates nothing, resolves no alias, creates no occurrence, and lays no Cable. root is a contextual keyword, so root = 5 is still an ordinary binding. A Voyage Plan may contain any number of bindings, but any other top-level statement, including the former input-bearing form BuildProduct[input], is InvalidRoot, as is a file with no root declaration or more than one. The declaration does not control codebase storage or visibility.

The plan is input, not the realized Cable. The Runtime validates and stores it through Vessel's Codebase-facing control surface. When a caller lays the target and sends an input, Vessel asks Carousel to commit each structure step that the input segment demands and publishes the result to the Cable data plane; the segment's Root occurrence is its first deduction demand. After decommissioning and drainage the Runtime composition layer returns a Fully Touchdown Cable, a canonical ordered list of hashes for the grounded leaves its segments actually reached, together with one ordered outcome per admitted input. Provenance keeps the reverse mapping to intermediate deductions so later voyages can reuse unchanged segments without mutating old records. See SCP-0004 and Laid Cables and Output Multiplicity.

The Runtime remains a logical participant until the laid Cable ends. Vessel owns the voyage, open occurrence frontier, structural demand, and deduction publication. Cable owns installed topology, channels, routed Values, Host emission sessions, and terminals. Scheduler still decides eligibility and outcomes; Host still supplies concrete computation. The Runtime is not merely a compiler that hands a completed Cable or generated Host program to a detached executor. This requirement does not prescribe deployment: both planes and Host may share one process, link as libraries, embed generated code, or communicate remotely. See SCP-0006 and SCP-0015.

docs.title: Runtime planes and live replanning
docs.text:
The complete deployment is the Subsea Cable Runtime, not Vessel alone:

Subsea Cable Runtime
├─ Vessel control plane
│  └─ Carousel — one requested atomic deduction
├─ Cable data plane
├─ Codebase and append-only deduction ledger
├─ Scheduler port
├─ Host port
└─ stateless result-composition layer

Vessel owns the voyage's still-open structural future. It tracks occurrences and the frontier, coordinates Scheduler demand and bounded speculation, asks Carousel to deduce one exact occurrence, commits the result, and publishes an append-only TopologyInstall to Cable. Carousel neither runs an autonomous voyage loop nor owns channels, outcomes, or Cable lifecycle.

Cable operates only topology it has atomically installed. It owns input admission, declaration-pin leases, channel capacity and backpressure, routed Values, the Outcome & Value Store, Host emission sessions, multiplicity checks, and terminal propagation. Cable never reads a mutable Goal alias or applies a reduction rule. Scheduler decides attempt and scope outcomes; Cable records and routes accepted outcomes and Values.

An Agent or operator authors replanning. After observing authorized Cable Values, outcomes, or terminals, it may store a new immutable Goal artifact and atomically rebind Name/Arity. An occurrence already committed to a hash never changes. A later undeduced occurrence—even in the same active segment—observes the alias only when Vessel demands its deduction, so it may select the new artifact. Vessel never invents this plan change from an outcome by itself.

The planes complete a segment together: Vessel must prove that no reachable structural work remains, and Cable must prove that installed work has drained. Only then may Cable propagate the segment's EndOfResult. After decommission, EndOfStream additionally requires structural publication to be closed and all segments and channels drained. A stateless Runtime composition layer combines Vessel provenance with Cable segment order and drainage evidence into the final result; outward adapters do not bypass it to read either plane's storage.

docs.title: Language Generic
docs.text:
Subsea Cable does not replace Java.

It does not replace Go.

It does not replace Rust.

It complements them.

Every language can become a Subsea consumer simply by implementing the specification.

.vyg

        ↓

Java
Go
Rust
Kotlin
Python
...

docs.title: Infrastructure Generic
docs.text:
Execution is not prescribed.

The same program may execute using

  • a sequential scheduler
  • a parallel scheduler
  • a distributed runtime
  • Kubernetes
  • Temporal
  • eBPF
  • custom schedulers

Subsea Cable intentionally leaves execution strategy outside of the language.

docs.title: Reduction, Deduction, and Evaluation
docs.text:
Subsea Cable separates three things that ordinary programs often collapse.

Reduction is the language rule that describes how a resolved Goal definition and its arguments produce subordinate structure or a leaf.

Deduction is the demand-driven Runtime event that resolves one Goal occurrence, applies its reduction rule, and commits the selected artifact hash and resulting structure. Deduction—not Touchdown—is the commit boundary.

Evaluation runs a concrete leaf after successive deductions have grounded it. Evaluation remains distinct from deduction.

An unqualified child exposed by one deduction is a new symbolic Name/Arity occurrence. Its position is committed, but its current alias is not resolved to an ArtifactHash until that child is itself demanded. The concrete Goal DAG is therefore disclosed incrementally rather than frozen in full before work begins.

docs.title: Goal Arrows and Function Arrows
docs.text:
A Goal arrow describes a structural reduction rule:

Upper = [] -> [A, B, C]
C = [b] -> [D[b], E]

Square brackets are serial composition. B depends on A and receives its result, while C likewise depends on B. When C is deduced, its reduction rule produces a serial structure that becomes conceptually [A, B, D, E], while lineage still records Upper.C.D and Upper.C.E.

A serial composition contains at least two elements and exports the Values of its final element. A routed stage runs once for every Value its predecessor emits, so [A, B] exports B's Values for every Value of A, and its output multiplicity follows the composition table in Goal signatures and output multiplicity. Earlier results are discarded unless they are routed explicitly.

Bare [] and singleton [A] are not expressions. This does not affect [] -> ..., which declares a zero-arity Goal, or Goal[], which is a deferred zero-argument Goal reference.

Curly braces with commas are parallel composition:

Upper = [x, y] -> { C[x], D[y] }

C[x] and D[y] have no dependency edge between them, so a Scheduler may run them concurrently. Braces permit concurrency but do not require simultaneous execution. A no-argument Goal is written as bare A inside a composition rather than A[] when it is an initial serial stage or a parallel sibling.

An unkeyed parallel composition exports no value. When followed by another serial element, the structure contains a dependency from the composite node to that element, but the language does not decide when the composite is considered satisfied. Goal names are never turned into result keys automatically:

[{A, B}, C[]] // C has a structural dependency on the parallel composite

An unkeyed parallel composition also requires at least two elements. Singleton {A} is invalid, while {} is an ordinary empty map value. Its output multiplicity is always /0, regardless of branch results: it publishes no outward Value and emits one composite EndOfResult.

A /0 predecessor invokes a routed successor zero times, and its empty segment completes normally:

[{A, B}, C[]]          // valid: runs once after {A, B}; C/0
[{A, B}, C[y]]         // valid: y comes from lexical scope
[{A, B}, C]            // valid: C is invoked zero times; the whole is /0
[{A, B}, [x] -> C[x]]  // valid: no parameter is bound; the whole is /0

NoOutput survives only as the internal absence of a scalar that a resolving-map binding or a function-leaf body explicitly requires, where it still reports NoOutputNotRoutable. It is not a runtime value: it is not null, unit, or an empty map, and it has no source literal. Empty channel segments are not NoOutput.

To pass parallel results downstream, every exported result needs an explicit key in a resolving map:

[
    [] -> {x: A, y: B},
    [{x, y}] -> [C[x], D[y]]
]

The keyed map is the direct body of a Goal arrow. Its branches are independent and expose one immutable map-shaped result {x: resultOfA, y: resultOfB}. The following Goal arrow receives that one value and destructures it. {A, B} alone can never provide values for [{x, y}] because it exports nothing.

A resolving map is still a value producer, not a Goal stage. It may never stand beside Goals in a composition:

[A, {x: B, y: C}, D]          // invalid
[A, [] -> {x: B, y: C}, D]    // valid; ignores A's output
[A, [i] -> {x: B[i], y: C[i]}, D] // valid; routes A's output

Only a map literal used as the direct body of a Goal arrow is a resolving map. Every other map is an ordinary value or selective lookup map. Resolving-map keys must be concrete, and every branch must have output multiplicity exactly /1. The map and a Goal arrow whose direct body it is are then /1. A /0 or /N branch reports OutputMultiplicityMismatch(expected = /1, context = resolving-map-branch) even when one invocation would emit a single Value; no first Value is chosen, no Values are collected, and no key is omitted. Singleton [] -> {x: A} is valid, while {} is always an ordinary empty map.

Bare downstream Goals are the one contextual shorthand: [A, B] means A/0 followed by B/1, with A's result as B's sole argument. Explicit brackets never receive an implicit argument:

[A[x], B]                         // B/1 receives A's result
[A[x], B[y]]                      // B structurally follows A and receives only y
[A[x], [Aresult] -> B[Aresult, y]] // B/2 receives both explicit values

The serial container still orders B[y] after A[x], but A's result is discarded unless it is forwarded explicitly through a Goal-arrow stage. No upstream value is automatically inserted or appended to a written argument list.

A downstream parallel composition has one narrowly defined implicit fan-out. It works only when every branch is a bare Goal with a unary implementation:

[A, {B, C}]

// exactly equivalent routing
[A, [i] -> {B[i], C[i]}]

The same one upstream value is sent to both branches. If either branch is not unary or needs any other value, all routing must be explicit:

[A, [i] -> {B[i], C[i, y]}]
[A, [i] -> {B[y], C[i]}]

A fully explicit parallel group ignores the upstream value while retaining the outer structural dependency:

[A, {B[a], C[b]}]

Implicit and explicit branches may not be mixed in one unkeyed parallel group. This fan-out shorthand never applies to resolving maps because maps cannot be composition stages. Keyed routing must be wrapped in a Goal arrow:

[A, [i] -> {x: B[i], y: C[i]}]

A Goal arrow may destructure and route one resolving-map result:

Distribute = [{x, y}] -> [T1[y], T2[x]]

A Goal-arrow body must be reduction structure. It cannot be a primitive, ordinary map value, or computed operator result. Valid direct forms are a Goal reference/call, an Anchor leaf/call, another Goal arrow, serial composition, unkeyed parallel composition, a resolving map, or an ordinary-map lookup whose selectable entries are all valid Goal structure. Ordinary value expressions remain valid inside Goal and Anchor argument lists, but those argument expressions may not themselves contain a value-producing Goal(...) or $anchor(...) call.

Value = [x] -> 42          // invalid: primitive body
Zero  = [x] -1> $host      // valid: Anchor/0; x is unused
Call  = [x] -1> $host(x)   // valid: Anchor/1
Bad   = [x] -> (y) -> y    // invalid: function arrow is never inline

A bare Anchor receives no implicit Goal parameters. $host and $host() are the same zero-argument occurrence. Signature compatibility and resolution belong to the Host, not structural validation. Serial and parallel elements follow the same structural restriction, so a value cannot stand beside Goals merely because it parses as an expression.

docs.title: Conditional structural pipelines
docs.text:
A pure selector expression may be followed by a keyed branch map as one structural pipeline:

CountDown = [n] -1> [
    n == 0,
    {
        true: Done[],
        false: CountDown[n - 1],
    },
]

CountDown declares -1> because its own recursive branch constrains its signature: without an explicit boundary the recursive component admits both /1 and /N, which is OutputMultiplicityCannotBeInferred(reason = recursive-signature-cycle).

Carousel evaluates n == 0 through the active Host primitive-semantics profile and exposes exactly one Goal-structure branch. The selector creates no Goal occurrence, leaf, or Scheduler work. The branch map is contextual structure: it is neither an ordinary value map nor a resolving map. It uses the ordinary normalized-key rules, including exact-match precedence and optional _ fallback. A missing match reports KeyNotFound in the existing phase.

All branches undergo structural validation, but an unselected branch creates no occurrence, resolves no alias, observes no routed value, and contributes no Touchdown. The selected branch's Values are the conditional pipeline's Values. Its output multiplicity joins the branch multiplicities: all /0 is /0, all /1 is /1, and any other known mix is /N. A branch whose multiplicity is unknown during authoring requires an explicit arrow on the containing named Goal.

The selector may contain parameters, immutable values, ordinary value maps/lookups, literals, and primitive operators. It may not contain a Goal or Anchor occurrence or call. The conditional pipeline receives no implicit upstream value; bind an upstream value with an enclosing Goal arrow before using it in the selector or branch arguments.

This conditional form has exactly two elements: the selector and the branch map, plus an optional trailing comma. [selector, {true: Left[], false: Right[]}, Next] is a syntax error. To continue after the selected branch, make the conditional pipeline one nested serial stage:

[
    [selector, {true: Left[], false: Right[]}],
    Next,
]

A bare uppercase Goal name is not a value selector. For example, if Flag is a Goal, [Flag, {true: Left[], false: Right[]}] reports UnboundName because Goal definitions never satisfy value lookup.

If the selector requires an unresolved routed value, the containing deduction stops at the conservative value barrier. It selects no key, creates no branch occurrence or observation, and commits no placeholder. Explicit demand reports DeductionBlocked(pendingValue); speculative consideration reports PrefetchBlocked until the value resolves.

The resolved selector is a value observation for SCP-0004 reuse. Provenance records a stable selector-value slot, its canonical digest, the normalized key selected, and the Host primitive profile. A prior selected-branch segment may be reused only when that digest and the other SCP-0004 identity inputs match; matching only the selected key is insufficient.

This contextual form is distinct from a reusable structure-valued ordinary map binding, whose general closure and routing rules remain a separate design question.

Outside a function-arrow leaf, an eager Goal call or Anchor call must itself be the direct structural occurrence: the complete Goal-arrow body, a serial or parallel element, or a resolving-map branch. It may not be hidden inside another call's arguments, a policy argument, an operator operand, a lookup key, or an ordinary value container.

[C[x], D]                 // valid: explicit dependency and routing
[C(x), [v] -> D[v]]       // valid: eager C is a visible stage
D[C(x)]                   // invalid: hidden eager Goal dependency
D[$fetch(x)]              // invalid: hidden Anchor effect
B[x + 1]                  // valid: effect-free primitive expression

The invalid nested forms report InvalidStructuralContext. Validation never invents a hoisted occurrence, and deduction never commits a placeholder while waiting for a hidden evaluation.

The square-bracket arrow remains structural and may appear inline in Goal composition. By contrast, a function arrow exists only as the complete leaf implementation of a named Goal:

Add = (x, y) -> x + y
Notify = ({x, y}) -> { $C(x); $D(y) }

(x, y) receives two arguments. ({x, y}) receives one map value and destructures it. The function composite uses semicolons to declare strict left-to-right dependencies. It does not forward non-final values and exposes the final value. It is not a map or a parallel Goal composition; ; is valid only inside this leaf implementation. Error handling remains Scheduler policy.

Function arrows have fixed arity with no default or variadic parameters. Destructuring requires one map containing every requested key. A non-map or a missing key produces DestructureMismatch; unrelated extra keys are allowed. Statically evident mismatches are validation errors, while dynamically known mismatches are deduction errors.

A function arrow is never a value. It cannot be anonymous inline content, aliased, passed, returned, stored in a map, used as an argument, or inserted as a stage such as [Goal1, (x) -> ..., Goal2].

Its body is the terminal content of its Goal and may use parameters, literals, operators, ordinary maps/lookups, and host calls written with Anchors. It may not reference or call another Subsea Goal at any depth. Therefore C(x) and C[x] are both invalid in a function body; Host Anchor calls must be written as $C(x) and $D(y). This keeps all Subsea-level composition in Goal arrows and pushes executable functions to the Goal graph's leaf boundary. Those Anchor calls do not create additional Subsea Goal nodes.

Subsea defines structure, not execution policy. Serial and parallel composition specify dependency edges, independence, value routing, and result keys. They do not specify success criteria, failure propagation, all/any/quorum completion, retry, cancellation, timeout, fire-and-forget behavior, or error aggregation. Those decisions belong to the Scheduler. A dependent evaluation instance can become eligible only when the Scheduler considers its upstream structure satisfied and supplies every value that the instance structurally requires.

docs.title: Laid Cables and Output Multiplicity
docs.text: A Goal is not a synchronous function. Subsea defines no call stack, generator, yield, lazy list, or channel value. An authorized outward caller asks the Runtime to lay a Goal target as a live Cable, sends inputs into its left end, and observes Values that leave its right end through the composition surface. Every authored Goal connection behaves as an implicit channel-equivalent edge. See SCP-0014.

docs.title: Laying, sending, and decommissioning
docs.text:
The outward Runtime operations are conceptually:

cable = lay(Eratosthenes/1)   // live Cable for a symbolic Name/inputArity
send(cable, [50])             // admit one complete input tuple
send(cable, [100])
decommision(cable)            // admit nothing more, drain, then EndOfStream

These are Runtime API operations, not Voyage expressions, and decommision is the owner-selected spelling. lay is a Vessel control operation that returns only after the voyage and Cable data-plane lifecycle both exist; sends, admission, pin leases, and decommision belong to Cable lifecycle. The resulting Cable handle is a Runtime capability, not a Subsea value: it cannot pass through a Map, a Goal argument, $Anchor(cable), a Host invocation, a StructureHash, or a memo key. A caller laying a stored Voyage Plan lays its root target by default; an authorized operator or debugger may lay any permitted Name/inputArity through the same operation. There is no one-shot evaluate(goal, arguments) and no input-bearing entry under another name, including lay + send + implicit decommision.

lay creates no evaluation segment, pins nothing, and resolves no alias. Each send checks the complete tuple arity, pins the Scheduler registry, the Host capability profile, and the forwarding allowlist, and then commits admission. That commit is the linearization point against decommision: a send that commits first becomes input segment Input(k), the next contiguous zero-based ordinal; a send that loses returns AdmissionClosed and releases its pins. A rejected send (AdmissionClosed, InputArityMismatch, ProfileNegotiationFailed) consumes no ordinal and creates no segment, occurrence, terminal, Cable member, or segment outcome. A slow pre-admission attempt never delays decommission drainage.

Pins belong to one input segment, not to the Cable, and each admitted segment keeps its pinned declaration snapshots resolvable until its terminal has propagated. Neither lay nor admission pins a codebase revision or resolves the laid target: its Root occurrence observes the alias only when demanded, so successive segments on one Cable may run different artifacts.

docs.title: One active input segment
docs.text:
Inputs are admitted in FIFO order and exactly one input segment is active at a time. Within it, Values flow downstream immediately and independent branches may run asynchronously. The next input begins only after the current segment's EndOfResult has propagated through the whole Cable and every operation it caused has drained. Until then the queued input receives no disclosure, deduction, alias observation, prefetch, or Host dispatch.

Runtime state has three isolation layers:

Layer State input segment declaration pins, occurrence and deduction namespace, attempts, routed Values, one EndOfResult laid Cable data plane input queue, installed topology, Outcome & Value Store, channel buffers and capacity, lifecycle and decommission state, completed segment order and drainage evidence Vessel control plane voyage, occurrence set, undeduced frontier, pending deductions and topology publication, Touchdown-window accounting shared Runtime services Codebase and alias index, append-only ledger backend, Scheduler and Host ports, any separately authorized Outcome Journal

A Value or outcome from one segment never satisfies a binding, value barrier, or occurrence in another.

Every edge is FIFO. Receiving from an empty live edge waits, sending to a full buffer waits, capacity 0 is a rendezvous, and silence is never termination. Capacity is Runtime-profile configuration with a profile default, not Voyage syntax or @policy; it changes blocking only, never results. It is independent of the SCP-0001 Touchdown prefetch window, and a send blocked on a full channel stays one active attempt.

docs.title: Terminals and results
docs.text:
EndOfResult(Succeeded | Failed(diagnostic) | Cancelled(diagnostic?)) ends one input segment while the Cable stays live. It is a control frame, not a value, and carries no identifier because segments never overlap. A successful segment may contain no Value; a Goal connected downstream is then invoked zero times. An unkeyed parallel composite emits exactly one EndOfResult for its whole scope; branch terminals remain internal.

A failed or cancelled segment ends only itself. Its published Values, effects, deduction records, and Touchdowns remain, and the next queued input proceeds normally after the terminal propagates and its work drains.

EndOfStream ends the whole Cable. Cable propagates it only after decommision, Vessel has closed structural publication, every admitted segment has reached its completion handshake, complete drainage, and propagation of the final EndOfResult. It carries no aggregate outcome. The final Cable result is the Fully Touchdown Cable plus one SegmentOutcome(Input(k), outcome) per admitted input in increasing Input(k) order.

docs.title: Goal signatures and output multiplicity
docs.text:
Every Goal signature has an output multiplicity:

GoalName / inputArity / outputMultiplicity

/0   success produces exactly zero Values       PrintLn/1/0
/1   success produces exactly one Value         ReadConfig/1/1
/N   success produces zero or more Values       Eratosthenes/1/N

Output multiplicity is part of the Goal's StructureHash, and therefore of its GoalNodeId, but not of the Name/Arity alias lookup key. One codebase revision cannot publish /0, /1, and /N overloads under one Name/inputArity, and a multiplicity change is a structural signature change.

A named Goal's plain -> asks for inference. It never defaults to /1. When inference cannot be unique, the named definition declares its contract with a multiplicity arrow:

Add          = (a, b) -> a + b                  // inferred /1
FanOut       = [x] -> {A[x], B[x]}              // inferred /0
Print        = [x] -0> $PrintLn(x)              // declared /0
ReadConfig   = [path] -1> $readConfig(path)     // declared /1
Eratosthenes = [limit] -N> $Eratosthenes(limit) // declared /N

The arrows -0>, -1>, and -N> are written without internal spaces and apply only to a named Goal's complete structural definition [params] -> .... A function-leaf definition (params) -> body always uses -> and is always /1; an inline Goal-arrow stage keeps -> and takes its body's multiplicity. The arrows are recognized only directly after a binding's leading [...] group, so x-1>0 and a parenthesized value such as (base)-1>0 keep their subtraction and comparison.

Inference may use a pure scalar function-arrow result (/1), the composite rules below, an explicit or uniquely inferred signature in the same source unit, and the signature of a hash-qualified artifact. It never uses the artifact an unqualified alias currently selects, a Host registry or capability snapshot, observed output counts, the branch one run selected, or Scheduler state.
